::: {.kw-overview}
This issue centres on how immunological compatibility and immunosuppression shape long-term graft survival. A Viennese exome-sequencing cohort shows that non-HLA molecular mismatch carries prognostic weight on a par with established HLA scores, while two immunosuppression papers — one reframing tacrolimus monitoring around the concentration-to-dose ratio, the other comparing everolimus with mycophenolate for post-transplant malignancy — both argue for individualised, exposure-aware dosing. On the rejection front, serial protocol biopsies document CD38-targeted daratumumab rescuing refractory antibody-mediated rejection in two children. Perioperative and preservation questions feature too: the intraoperative Surgical Apgar Score predicts delayed graft function, and the first paediatric experience with hypothermic oxygenated machine perfusion suggests longer, safer cold-preservation windows are achievable. Two cardiometabolic studies close the issue — a negative randomised trial of urate-lowering on left ventricular mass in living donors, and a large meta-analysis of bariatric surgery as a route to transplant access.
:::

---

### 1. [The combined impact of HLA and non-HLA mismatch between donors and recipients on kidney transplant survival: a genomic analysis in a prospective cohort](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ebiom.2026.106420)
[Kammer M, Heinzel A, Shoebridge S, Reindl-Schwaighofer R, Hu K, Chen HS, Kainz A, Daoudi I, David AF, Fischer G, Keating B, Niemann M, Oberbauer R, et al. *EBioMedicine*, 2026. PMID: 42556135.]{.kw-ref}

This prospective single-centre study at the Vienna General Hospital sequenced the exomes of deceased-donor kidney transplant pairs recruited between January 2012 and June 2023, with 1,187 of 1,209 pairs passing quality control. The authors quantified non-HLA incompatibility with a score counting non-synonymous single-nucleotide variants that encode trans-membrane or secreted kidney proteins (2,371 of 20,421 human proteins qualified), then tested it against graft loss in adjusted Cox models. Replicating their earlier work in recipients with primary function at 90 days, each interquartile-range increase in the non-HLA score carried a hazard ratio for graft loss of 1.33 (95% CI 1.02–1.74). Crucially, the non-HLA score was essentially uncorrelated with conventional eplet mismatch (Spearman 0.02, p=0.47), implying the two capture different immunological risk. A composite of the two scores was associated with graft loss at a hazard ratio of 1.76 (95% CI 1.20–2.57), translating to a 0.52-year difference in 7-year restricted mean survival time between the lowest and highest quartiles (95% CI 0.16–0.87). The investigators conclude that non-HLA mismatch matters to roughly the same degree as HLA-region mismatch and might eventually help calibrate how much maintenance immunosuppression a given pairing needs. For UK practice this reinforces the case for looking beyond HLA when stratifying immunological risk, though the score remains a research tool pending external validation.

### 2. [Beyond Trough Levels: Tacrolimus Dose Requirements and Individualized Monitoring in Kidney Transplantation](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ajt.2026.07.031)
[Reuter S, Kuypers DRJ. *Am J Transplant*, 2026. PMID: 42551532.]{.kw-ref}

This review makes the case that the tacrolimus trough concentration, while indispensable, says nothing about the dose needed to reach it, and that the concentration-to-dose (C/D) ratio supplies that missing denominator as a cheap, time-varying dose-requirement phenotype derived from routine bloods. A low C/D ratio identifies "fast metabolisers" with high dose requirements, and the authors summarise registry-scale evidence linking low C/D to impaired graft function, rejection, BK virus complications, graft failure, and death, with risk rising in graded fashion as the ratio falls. They also note a more favourable trajectory when a low C/D normalises over time than when it stays persistently low, suggesting the phenotype is dynamic rather than fixed. The proposed role is risk stratification and triage to more intensive area-under-curve exposure assessment, not a stand-alone dosing algorithm. The authors are careful to flag that interpretation depends on valid sampling, assay, timing, and formulation, and that no trial has yet shown a C/D-guided intervention improves outcomes. For UK units, the practical takeaway is that the dose already recorded alongside every trough is an underused, no-cost signal for flagging higher-risk recipients who may warrant closer surveillance.

### 3. [Risk of post-transplant malignancy: a single center retrospective comparative study between everolimus and mycophenolate in kidney transplant recipients](https://doi.org/10.1093/joneph/aajag211)
[Stefanelli LF, Cacciapuoti M, Alessi M, Silvestre C, Martino FK, Del Prete D, Calò LA, Nalesso F. *J Nephrol*, 2026. PMID: 42544510.]{.kw-ref}

Set against the backdrop that malignancy-related mortality after transplantation has not improved in step with cardiovascular and infectious deaths, this retrospective study from Padova University Hospital compared de novo cancer risk in 159 kidney transplant recipients grafted between 2015 and 2018, stratified by whether maintenance used the mTOR inhibitor everolimus or mycophenolate, over a mean follow-up of about seven years. Fifty-four recipients developed de novo cancers, most commonly non-melanoma skin cancer, and there was no significant difference in malignancy incidence between the everolimus and mycophenolate groups. On multivariable analysis the drivers of cancer were older age, hepatitis C, and a pre-transplant malignancy history rather than the choice of agent. Patient and graft survival were numerically higher in the mycophenolate group, while the rejection rate was numerically lower with everolimus, neither reaching significance. The headline is that switching to an mTOR inhibitor did not deliver the anticipated reduction in de novo cancer relative to mycophenolate in this cohort. The authors suggest that, in carefully selected older recipients, individualised immunosuppression minimisation may be a more rational lever on cancer risk than agent substitution — a nuance worth weighing given the small, single-centre design.

### 4. [Treatment response to daratumumab in antibody-mediated kidney allograft rejection: evidence from serial protocol biopsies](https://doi.org/10.1093/ckj/sfag236)
[Kanzelmeyer NK, Verboom M, Hallensleben M, Bade-Döding C, Schön A, Haffner D, Bräsen JH, Melk A. *Clin Kidney J*, 2026. PMID: 42553987.]{.kw-ref}

This paper pairs a literature review with two paediatric cases of refractory antibody-mediated rejection followed by serial protocol biopsies over 10–12 months, treated with the anti-CD38 monoclonal daratumumab (16 mg/kg, five weekly induction doses then maintenance every two to four weeks). In a 10-year-old girl with recurrent rejection despite prior rituximab and immunoglobulin, donor-specific antibody fell from a mean fluorescence intensity of 2,425 to undetectable, C4d staining turned negative, glomerulitis resolved, and albuminuria dropped from 1,153 to 8 mg/g creatinine as the biopsy shifted from active to predominantly chronic changes. In a 9-year-old boy with severe transplant glomerulopathy, donor-specific antibody fell from 26,069 to 8,614, albuminuria improved from 4,308 to 1,174 mg/g, and the 10-month biopsy showed complete histological resolution of active disease with under 1% fibrosis. Both children maintained stable graft function with no serious adverse events, the main toxicity being hypogammaglobulinaemia requiring immunoglobulin replacement alongside co-trimoxazole prophylaxis. The authors position CD38-directed plasma-cell depletion as a rational rescue option for late, donor-specific-antibody-driven rejection, while stressing that this is only two retrospective cases. For UK teams facing refractory AMR — where evidence-based options are thin — this adds to a growing signal that controlled paediatric and adult trials of daratumumab are needed.

### 5. [The Surgical Apgar Score is Associated with Delayed Graft Function after Deceased-Donor Kidney Transplantation: A Retrospective Cohort](https://doi.org/10.34067/KID.0000001270)
[Von Tokarski F, Labro M, Soorojebally Y, Trillat B, Lefebvre M, Kossari N, Eddine AJ, Pelle G, Tricot L, Delahousse M, Oniszczuk J, Le Guen M, Hertig A. *Kidney360*, 2026. PMID: 42560772.]{.kw-ref}

This single-centre retrospective cohort tested whether the Surgical Apgar Score — a simple 10-point intraoperative composite of lowest heart rate, lowest mean arterial pressure, and estimated blood loss — predicts delayed graft function in 301 consecutive adult deceased-donor kidney transplant recipients operated between 2016 and 2021. A low score (≤7) was present in 95 recipients (32%), and delayed graft function, defined as dialysis within seven days, occurred in 79 (26%). On multivariable logistic regression, a low Surgical Apgar Score was independently associated with delayed graft function (OR 2.05, 95% CI 1.16–3.61), alongside longer dialysis vintage (OR 1.05 per 6 months, 95% CI 1.01–1.10), absence of renin-angiotensin system inhibitor therapy (OR 2.27, 95% CI 1.27–4.00), and longer cold ischaemia time (OR 1.11 per 2 hours, 95% CI 1.02–1.21). Estimated intraoperative blood loss was the dominant contributor to a low score. The appeal for UK teams is that this score is available to the anaesthetist and surgeon the moment the operation ends, flagging recipients who may need closer early monitoring; the authors highlight blood loss and intraoperative haemodynamics as potentially modifiable targets, though the single-centre, retrospective design limits causal inference.

### 6. [Extending Preservation in Pediatric Kidney Transplantation: First Contemporary Experience With Hypothermic Oxygenated Machine Perfusion](https://doi.org/10.1111/aor.70196)
[Spagnoletti G, Favi E, Mauro A, Fratti AM, Cirelli R, Maistri M, Cappoli A, Labbadia R, Gargiulo A, Busutti M, Guzzo I, Spada M. *Artif Organs*, 2026. PMID: 42552654.]{.kw-ref}

Machine perfusion is now standard for adult deceased-donor kidneys but paediatric experience with hypothermic oxygenated machine perfusion (HOPE) has been minimal, which this single-centre retrospective analysis sets out to address. Of 129 paediatric transplants performed between November 2019 and December 2023, the 92 deceased-donor recipients (mean age 12.6 ± 5.9 years, 59.8% male) were split into 40 preserved with HOPE and 52 with static cold storage. Despite a markedly longer total cold preservation time in the HOPE group (23.7 ± 4.1 versus 13.3 ± 3.7 hours; p<0.001), there were no significant differences in delayed graft function, biopsy-proven acute rejection, postoperative length of stay, or graft function to one year. One-year death-censored graft survival was essentially identical at 97% for HOPE and 98% for static cold storage. The authors conclude that HOPE is safe and feasible in children even when cold-preservation times are prolonged, which could ease the logistics of matching paediatric donors and recipients across distance. For UK paediatric programmes weighing perfusion technology, the reassurance that longer preservation did not translate into worse early outcomes is the practical signal, tempered by the small, non-randomised comparison.

### 7. [A Randomized Controlled Trial to Evaluate Allopurinol vs Placebo on Left Ventricular Mass in Living Kidney Donors](https://doi.org/10.34067/KID.0000001313)
[Langberg NE, Jenssen TG, Hopp E, Haugen A, Åsberg A, Birkeland KI, Hartmann A, Dahle DO. *Kidney360*, 2026. PMID: 42545761.]{.kw-ref}

Prompted by concern that living kidney donation may carry long-term cardiovascular risk, and that elevated uric acid tracks with left ventricular mass, this single-centre phase 2b trial randomised 71 healthy donors (aged 18 or over, eGFR above 30, at least six months after nephrectomy) 1:1 to allopurinol 300 mg daily or placebo, double-blind, for nine months, with change in left ventricular mass on cardiac MRI as the primary outcome. Allopurinol lowered uric acid as expected (p<0.001), but there was no significant difference in left ventricular mass change between arms: −0.25 (± 4.4) g with allopurinol versus 1.04 (± 4.2) g with placebo (p=0.25). There was likewise no effect on blood pressure (p=0.98) or insulin sensitivity (p=0.62). Adverse events were more frequent on allopurinol, occurring in 18 of the treatment group (70%) versus 10 on placebo (37%), with all three severe events in the allopurinol arm. This is a clearly negative trial: urate-lowering did not improve a cardiovascular surrogate in donors despite hitting its biochemical target. For UK donor follow-up, it argues against reaching for allopurinol as cardioprotection in normouricaemic donors and is a useful counterweight to enthusiasm for urate-lowering on cardiovascular grounds.

### 8. [Safety and Effectiveness of Metabolic and Bariatric Surgery Before and After Kidney Transplantation: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11695-026-08878-w)
[Abudukadi G, Song ZH, Azhati Y, Maimaiti M, Nuermaimaiti M, Tulading A, He R, Lv CH, Wang MJ, Yasheng R, Zeng H, Keranmu G, Anvarbek K, Munisa K, Tuxun T. *Obes Surg*, 2026. PMID: 42560441.]{.kw-ref}

Obesity is both a barrier to listing and a threat to transplant success, and this systematic review and meta-analysis — searching six databases to February 2026 and pooling 49 studies covering 1,504 adult kidney transplant candidates or recipients — asks whether metabolic and bariatric surgery helps. Among the 1,215 patients undergoing surgery before transplantation, the pooled waitlisting rate was 78.0% (95% CI 66.0–88.0%; I²=90.3%) and the transplantation rate was 52.0% (95% CI 36.0–68.0%; I²=96.3%), with one-year graft survival exceeding 99% (95% CI 98–100%; I²=17.5%). In the smaller post-transplant surgery group (289 patients), diabetes improved in 93% (95% CI 64–100%) and hypertension in 92% (95% CI 54–100%), defined as medication reduction or biochemical improvement. Waitlisting rates differed significantly by country (p<0.001) but not by procedure type (p=0.09), and the authors are candid that the evidence is overwhelmingly observational with very high heterogeneity, leaving comparative safety and long-term graft effects uncertain. For UK services, where a BMI threshold often stalls listing, this supports bariatric surgery as a credible pathway back onto the waiting list for selected patients, while underlining the absence of controlled comparative data.
